existingApplication.title: Help With an Existing or Stalled Connecticut Medicaid Application

blocks.text: Already Applied? You May Not Have to Start Over.

You submitted a Connecticut Medicaid application. Now DSS is asking for more information, the application is still pending, documents are difficult to track, or you simply are not sure what happens next.
Compass Title19 Consultants LLC helps Connecticut individuals, families and caregivers navigate existing Medicaid applications, including HUSKY C and Long-Term Services & Supports (LTSS) cases.

After reviewing the circumstances and the documents already submitted, Compass may be able to help identify outstanding administrative requirements, organize requested verifications, assist with appropriate DSS follow-up and bring structure to a process that has become difficult to manage.
You do not necessarily have to abandon an application simply because the process has become complicated.
Schedule an Existing Medicaid Application Review
When a Medicaid Application Becomes Difficult to Manage
A Medicaid application can begin simply and become complicated after submission.
Families often contact Compass because:
DSS has requested additional verification or documentation
The application has been pending and the family does not know its current status
Bank statements or financial records are incomplete or difficult to organize
DSS has questions about financial transactions
A nursing facility is asking the family for an application update
A family member started the application but can no longer manage it
Several people have been involved and no one knows exactly what was submitted
A deadline is approaching
The applicant has received multiple DSS notices
The family is unsure who the assigned worker is
Documents were submitted but the family is unsure whether they were received or associated with the case
The applicant's circumstances changed while the application was pending

The appropriate next step depends on the specific application and notices involved. Compass begins by reviewing what has already happened rather than assuming a new application is automatically required.
What Does 'Stalled' Mean?

“Stalled” is not an official Connecticut DSS case status. Compass uses the term informally to describe an application that a client believes is not moving forward as expected or has become difficult to manage.

A pending application may still be under review. DSS may be waiting for requested information, reviewing submitted documentation, assigning or processing the case, or addressing another eligibility issue.

For pending LTSS applications, Connecticut DSS states that applicants receive contact information for the worker assigned to the application and may contact that worker regarding case-specific questions.
Before assuming that an application is lost or needs to be restarted, it is important to understand its actual status.
What Compass Does First
We Review the Existing Case
When appropriate, the first step is to understand what has already been submitted and what DSS has communicated.
Depending on the case and scope of engagement, Compass may review:
The original Medicaid or LTSS application, if available
DSS notices and correspondence
Verification requests
Documents previously submitted
Financial records relevant to outstanding requests
Application dates and known deadlines
Caseworker or DSS contact information
Information from the nursing facility or other involved professionals
Authorization or representative documentation
Other materials relevant to the pending application
This review helps us determine what administrative assistance Compass may be able to provide and whether another professional should become involved.
Received a DSS Verification Request?
The Entire Notice Matters.

Connecticut DSS may ask applicants to provide proof of information used to determine eligibility. DSS publishes a Guide to Verification of Information that provides examples of documents that may be accepted, while noting that applicants should speak with their worker if they do not have one of the listed forms of proof.
A verification request should be read carefully, including all pages, requested items and deadlines.
Compass can help clients within our scope by:
Reviewing the administrative request
Breaking the request into manageable categories
Identifying documentation the client already has
Helping organize responsive records
Identifying items that may still need to be obtained
Preparing an organized submission package
Maintaining a record of documents provided
Assisting with appropriate administrative follow-up
When you meet with Compass, provide the entire DSS notice and any attachments—not only the first page.
Get Help With a DSS Verification Request →
What If Documents Are Missing?
Missing a particular document does not necessarily mean that nothing can be done.

Connecticut DSS's verification guidance explains that if an applicant does not have one of the commonly listed forms of proof, the applicant should speak with the worker about other forms of verification that may be acceptable.
Compass can help identify the gap, organize available information and assist the client in addressing the administrative request within our scope.
We do not create, alter or misrepresent documentation. Information provided to DSS should be accurate and complete.
What If DSS Is Asking About Bank Transactions?

LTSS cases can involve extensive financial review. Connecticut DSS states that certain skilled nursing facility and Home and Community-Based Services applications require a five-year income and asset review depending on the applicant's prior Medicaid status.
A request involving transfers, deposits, withdrawals or other financial activity may therefore require additional explanation or supporting documentation.
Compass can assist with organizing records and identifying documentation relevant to an administrative request.

However, when a transaction raises legal questions involving gifts, transfers, trusts, property ownership, estate planning or legal asset-protection strategies, Compass may recommend consultation with a qualified elder-law attorney.
Do not create explanations, move money, transfer property or alter ownership solely because you believe it will resolve a Medicaid issue without first obtaining appropriate individualized guidance.
Can Compass Communicate With DSS?
When the appropriate authorization is in place and the service is included in the engagement, Compass may assist with administrative communication and follow-up concerning a client's Medicaid case.

Connecticut DSS allows applicants to designate representatives to assist with the application and eligibility process. The appropriate authorization depends on the circumstances and the type of assistance requested.
Compass will determine what authorization is appropriate before requesting or discussing protected case information with DSS.
How Compass Can Help With an Existing Application
Case Status Review
We help organize the information available about the application and identify known outstanding administrative issues.
DSS Notice Review
We review relevant DSS correspondence and help clients understand what is being requested within our non-attorney scope.
Verification Organization
We help gather and organize documentation responsive to DSS requests.
Financial Record Organization
For applicable cases, we assist with organizing bank statements and other financial records relevant to the Medicaid eligibility review.
Existing LTSS Applications
We may assist families with pending nursing-home Medicaid or HCBS/LTSS applications after reviewing the case and determining the appropriate scope.
Existing HUSKY C Applications
We may assist with HUSKY C applications that are already underway, including outstanding verification and administrative follow-up.
Authorized Representative Support
When properly authorized, Compass may assist with appropriate administrative communications with DSS.
Application Follow-Up
We help clients maintain an organized record of outstanding items, submissions and relevant follow-up.
Professional Referrals
If the case presents legal, tax, investment, financial or other issues outside our scope, we recommend that the client consult the appropriate qualified professional.
Ask Compass to Review Your Existing Application →
What Compass Cannot Promise
Compass cannot guarantee that DSS will approve an application, determine eligibility by a particular date, accept a particular explanation or document, or reach a specific outcome.
Connecticut DSS is responsible for Medicaid eligibility determinations.

Compass also cannot promise that every existing application can or should continue exactly as filed. After reviewing a case, there may be circumstances that require correction, additional documentation, a different administrative step or advice from another professional.
Our role is to provide organized, knowledgeable Medicaid administrative support within our scope—not to guarantee a government decision.
Do I Need to Start a New Application?
Not necessarily.
One of the reasons to review an existing case first is to determine what has already occurred.
Submitting a duplicate or unnecessary application without understanding the status of the existing one can create additional confusion.
Compass does not automatically recommend starting over. We first review the information available and determine what administrative next steps appear appropriate within our scope.
If a new application is appropriate, we can discuss that after the existing situation has been assessed.
Pending Nursing Home Medicaid or LTSS Application?

Connecticut DSS currently processes new skilled nursing facility and intermediate care facility Medicaid applications through designated LTSS Application Centers based on the location of the facility.
New Medicaid applications for home- and community-based waiver services are processed statewide through the Greater Hartford LTSS Application Center.
DSS states that applicants with questions specific to a pending LTSS case may contact the assigned caseworker. Once a case is assigned, the applicant is provided the worker's contact information.
Compass can help clients organize their case information before administrative follow-up and, when appropriately authorized, may assist with communication within the scope of the engagement.
Get Help With a Pending LTSS Application →
What About Renewals and Interim Changes?
New LTSS applications and existing-benefit maintenance are not always handled through the same workflow.
Connecticut DSS states that LTSS Application Centers process new applications, while renewals and interim changes continue through the statewide ConneCT model.

If your issue concerns an existing Medicaid recipient rather than a new pending application, Compass can determine whether the matter is better handled as a renewal, redetermination, reported change or another administrative process.
Get Help With a Medicaid Renewal or Redetermination →
Before Your Existing-Application Consultation
To make the review as productive as possible, gather what you already have. You do not need to reconstruct the entire case before contacting Compass.
Helpful materials may include:
All recent DSS notices and letters
A copy of the application, if available
Verification requests
Copies of documents already submitted
Any confirmation or record showing when documents were submitted
Caseworker information, if assigned
Relevant nursing-facility correspondence
Any authorization or representative documents already on file
A simple timeline of important events, if known
Do not delay contacting Compass merely because some documents are missing. We can determine what is needed after the initial review.
Detailed individualized Medicaid guidance and case work are provided pursuant to Compass's consultation and engagement process.
Why Choose Compass for an Existing Medicaid Application?
Experience With Connecticut Medicaid Administration
Compass Title19 Consultants LLC was founded by Akua Achiaa Okyere, MBA, a former Connecticut Department of Social Services eligibility professional.
Her DSS experience included Medicaid eligibility work, complex case resolution, policy and procedure, staff training, quality assurance and eligibility operations.
That background informs Compass's structured approach to reviewing Medicaid applications, documentation and administrative requirements.
We Do Not Assume You Have to Start Over
We begin by understanding the existing case and what has already been done.
We Help Bring Order to the Documentation
When multiple notices, statements and submissions have accumulated, organization matters.
We Know Our Professional Boundaries
When a case requires legal, tax, investment, financial or other licensed professional advice, Compass encourages collaboration with the appropriate professional.
Connecticut Is Our Focus
Compass focuses on Connecticut Medicaid, including HUSKY C, LTSS, nursing-home Medicaid and applicable home- and community-based services.
Compass Is Not a Law Firm
Compass Title19 Consultants LLC is a non-attorney Medicaid consulting and care management organization.
We provide Medicaid education, application and documentation assistance, administrative navigation, DSS verification support and related services within our professional scope.

We do not provide legal advice or replace an attorney. Matters involving trusts, estate planning, legal asset-protection strategies, significant transfers, property rights, legal appeals or other legal issues should be addressed with an appropriate attorney.
Compass welcomes collaboration with elder-law attorneys, nursing facilities, care managers, financial professionals and other professionals serving Connecticut families.
Frequently Asked Questions

Yes, depending on the circumstances. Compass can review the existing application and determine what administrative assistance we may be able to provide.

Not automatically. We recommend understanding the status of the existing application before deciding whether another application is appropriate.

Yes, depending on the circumstances and the issue involved.

No. Connecticut DSS determines Medicaid eligibility and application outcomes.

article01.title: Can I Own a Home and Qualify for Medicaid in Connecticut?

blocks.text: Yes - in many situations, owning a home does not automatically prevent you from qualifying for Connecticut Medicaid.

But the complete answer depends on which Medicaid program you are applying for, whether you are seeking Long-Term Services & Supports (LTSS), your equity interest in the property, who lives in the home, and what happens to the property before and after eligibility.

That distinction matters. Families sometimes hear “you can keep your house” and assume the home can never affect Medicaid. Others hear “Medicaid will take your house” and panic unnecessarily. Neither statement tells the whole story.
Here is what Connecticut families should understand.
1. Owning a Home Does Not Automatically Disqualify You

For Medicaid eligibility purposes, a person's principal residence can receive special treatment under Medicaid rules. In Connecticut long-term-care cases, the home may not be treated the same way as cash, a checking account or another countable resource.
That means a person should not assume that home ownership alone makes them ineligible for HUSKY C or Medicaid LTSS.

However, the rules are different depending on the Medicaid coverage group and the person's circumstances. This article focuses particularly on long-term-care Medicaid, where home equity and transfer rules can become especially important.
2. Home Equity Can Matter for Medicaid LTSS
For 2026, Connecticut's published LTSS standards list an excess home-equity limit of $1,130,000 for an institutionalized individual.
Home equity is not necessarily the same as the property's market value. In general terms, equity is the value of the person's ownership interest after debts secured by the property are considered.

Connecticut also identifies important exceptions to the LTSS home-equity limitation. For example, the limit does not apply in the same way when a spouse, a child under age 21, or an adult child who is blind or disabled is lawfully residing in the home.
Because this dollar amount is subject to change, families should check the current Connecticut DSS standard rather than relying on an older article.
Important: a home being treated favorably for eligibility purposes does not mean that every later issue involving the home disappears.
3. What If My Spouse Still Lives in the Home?
Married couples have special Medicaid protections when one spouse needs institutional long-term care and the other remains in the community.

Connecticut's long-term-care guidance recognizes protections for a primary residence when the community spouse continues to live there. Other financial protections may also apply to the spouse remaining in the community.
This is one reason married couples should not assume that they must sell the home or impoverish the spouse at home before applying for Medicaid.
The couple's complete financial situation still matters, and current community-spouse rules should be reviewed before major financial or property decisions are made.
4. What If I Enter a Nursing Home?
Moving into a nursing facility does not automatically mean that a home must immediately be sold.

The Medicaid treatment of the home can depend on factors including the applicant's ownership interest, equity, intent and household circumstances, as well as whether certain qualifying relatives remain in the property.
The more important point is this: do not make a rushed decision about selling, gifting or changing ownership of a home simply because a nursing-home admission has occurred.
A property decision can affect Medicaid, taxes, estate planning and legal rights at the same time.
5. Be Very Careful About Giving Away or Transferring the Home

For many Medicaid LTSS cases, Connecticut applies a five-year review of income and assets. Transfer rules can apply when an institutionalized person or spouse disposes of assets for less than fair market value during the applicable look-back period.
A home is not automatically outside those transfer rules.

There are specific circumstances in which a home may be transferred without a Medicaid transfer penalty - for example, certain transfers to a spouse, a child under age 21, a blind or disabled child, and other narrowly defined family situations.
Those exceptions have detailed requirements. A family should not assume that a relative qualifies simply because the relative lives in the house or provides some assistance.

Before transferring a deed, adding someone to title, gifting a property interest or selling for less than fair market value, obtain individualized advice from an appropriate elder-law attorney. Compass does not provide legal advice or prepare deeds.
6. Eligibility and Estate Recovery Are Different Questions
One of the most important distinctions families should understand is that Medicaid eligibility and Medicaid estate recovery are not the same issue.
A home may receive favorable treatment while a person is alive and applying for benefits, yet later raise estate-recovery or probate questions depending on the circumstances.
Therefore, the question “Can I qualify while owning my home?” should not be treated as identical to “What will happen to my home after I die?”

Estate recovery, probate, trusts, deeds and estate planning involve legal issues. Compass can explain the Medicaid administrative context, but an elder-law or estate-planning attorney should provide individualized legal advice.
7. What About Home and Community-Based Services?
Connecticut Medicaid LTSS is not limited to nursing-home care. DSS also provides pathways for qualifying home and community-based services.

Home ownership does not automatically prevent someone from exploring HCBS. However, the applicable Medicaid financial rules, functional eligibility requirements and program criteria still need to be considered.

wisdomArticles.title: Can I Own a Home and Qualify for Medicaid in Connecticut?

blocks.text: A home is often a family's largest asset—and one of the first things people worry about when long-term care and Medicaid enter the conversation.
The short answer

Yes—in many cases, a person can own a home and qualify for Connecticut Medicaid. But the answer depends on the Medicaid coverage group, the person's living arrangement, home equity, who lives in the home and other facts.
Why the home is different from cash

Medicaid distinguishes countable assets from assets that may be excluded under program rules. A principal residence can receive special treatment, so families should not assume that owning a home automatically prevents LTSS eligibility.
Home equity matters

For institutional LTSS, federal and Connecticut rules can limit eligibility when an applicant's equity interest in the home exceeds the applicable home-equity standard. These standards can change, which is why Compass recommends checking the current DSS program standards rather than relying on an old online figure.
A spouse at home changes the analysis

When one spouse needs nursing-home Medicaid and the other remains in the community, special spousal protections may apply. The home and certain financial resources can be treated differently than they would be for a single applicant.
Do not give the house away just to qualify

A transfer of a home for less than fair market value can create Medicaid consequences unless an exception applies. Connecticut policy includes specific exceptions in certain circumstances, but deeds, gifts, trusts and property transfers are legal matters that should be reviewed with a qualified elder-law attorney.
Estate recovery is a separate issue

Eligibility today and possible estate recovery later are different questions. A home can sometimes be excluded for eligibility purposes while still raising later estate-recovery considerations. Families should not treat the word “exempt” as meaning “protected forever.”

wisdomArticles.title: What Is Connecticut's Medicaid Five-Year Look-Back?

blocks.text: The phrase “five-year look-back” can make families fear that every financial decision made during the last five years will cause a Medicaid problem. The rule is more nuanced.
What the five-year review means

Connecticut DSS explains that applicable HUSKY C LTSS cases can require a five-year income and asset review. The review helps DSS understand financial history and determine whether program rules affecting LTSS eligibility and payment have been met.
It is not an automatic five-year penalty

The look-back does not mean every transaction during five years is improper. DSS may review transfers, withdrawals, closed accounts, property transactions and other activity to understand where assets went and whether fair value was received.
Transfers can require closer review

Transfers for less than fair market value can affect Medicaid LTSS. Exceptions may apply in particular circumstances, so families should avoid assuming that every gift creates a penalty—or that a transfer is harmless because it happened several years ago.
Documentation is essential

Bank statements, check images, receipts, closing statements, invoices, contracts and records explaining significant transactions can be important. The clearer the paper trail, the easier it is to respond accurately to a verification request.
Avoid last-minute asset moves

Do not move money, change a deed or give away property simply because Medicaid may be needed. Those actions can create complications. Legal questions involving gifts, trusts, deeds or asset-protection strategies belong with an elder-law attorney.

wisdomArticles.title: What Happens When One Spouse Needs Nursing-Home Medicaid?

blocks.text: When one spouse needs nursing-home care, couples often worry that the spouse remaining at home will lose everything. Medicaid LTSS includes important protections, but the rules require careful documentation.
Marriage does not mean both spouses must become impoverished

Medicaid LTSS includes protections for a spouse who remains in the community while the other spouse receives institutional long-term care. These rules are designed to preserve certain resources and income for the community spouse.
Resources are reviewed as a couple

For married LTSS applicants, DSS reviews the couple's financial circumstances under spousal-impoverishment rules. The amount a community spouse may retain is governed by current program standards and the facts of the case.
Income is not treated exactly like assets

A community spouse may have protections involving income as well as resources. The calculation can be fact-specific, so a couple should not assume that all income must be turned over to the nursing facility.
The home can receive special treatment

A principal residence may be treated differently when the community spouse continues to live there. Property ownership, transfers, trusts and estate planning can involve legal issues and should be reviewed by qualified counsel when needed.
Prepare records early

Couples should gather statements for bank, retirement and investment accounts, property information, income verification and insurance records. Early organization helps establish an accurate financial picture.

wisdomArticles.title: Medicare vs. Medicaid: Who Pays for Long-Term Care?

blocks.text: A short rehabilitation stay can quickly turn into a long-term-care discussion. Understanding who pays—and for how long—helps families plan before a coverage transition becomes a crisis.
They are not interchangeable

Medicare and Medicaid are different programs. Medicare is primarily federal health insurance, while Medicaid is a needs-based federal-state program that can cover long-term services and supports for eligible people.
Medicare may cover qualifying short-term skilled care

Medicare can cover skilled nursing facility care when its coverage requirements are met, but it does not generally pay indefinitely for custodial long-term care simply because a person needs ongoing help.
Medicaid can be a long-term-care payer
Connecticut Medicaid LTSS can cover eligible nursing-facility care and qualifying home and community-based services. Financial and functional requirements vary by pathway.
Why families get caught off guard

A rehabilitation stay can begin under Medicare and later reach a point where Medicare coverage ends or changes. Families may then need to consider private payment, long-term-care insurance, Medicaid or another source.
Plan before the transition
Ask the facility what is paying today, what could change, what notices may be issued and what information is needed if a Medicaid application becomes necessary.

wisdomArticles.title: What Happens When DSS Requests Five Years of Bank Statements?

blocks.text: A request for years of bank statements can feel overwhelming. Breaking the request into accounts, periods and transactions makes the task much more manageable.
The request has a purpose
In applicable LTSS cases, DSS may need a multi-year financial history. Bank statements help establish assets, income patterns, account ownership and transactions that may need explanation.
Start with an account inventory
List every account held during the requested period, including accounts that were closed. Record the financial institution, account type, ownership and approximate open/close dates.
Request missing records promptly
Older statements can take time to retrieve. Contact the bank early and ask what historical records, check images and transaction details remain available.
Flag—not hide—unusual transactions

Large withdrawals, checks, transfers, deposits and property-related transactions may need supporting records. Organize receipts or explanations rather than assuming DSS will understand the transaction from the statement alone.

wisdomArticles.title: What Is a HUSKY C Medical Spend-Down?

blocks.text: Receiving a HUSKY C spend-down notice can be confusing, especially when a person thought Medicaid was either approved or denied. Spend-down is a distinct eligibility pathway.
A spend-down is an eligibility pathway
Connecticut DSS explains that some HUSKY C applicants whose income is above the applicable limit may still qualify through a medical spend-down if other eligibility requirements are met.
Think of it as an amount that must be met with qualifying medical expenses
A spend-down is often compared with an insurance deductible. DSS establishes the spend-down and qualifying medical expenses can be used toward meeting it under program rules.
It is not simply spending cash until assets are low
Income spend-down and asset eligibility are different concepts. A person can have a medical spend-down and still need to meet the applicable asset and non-financial requirements.
Keep medical bills and proof
Because medical expenses matter, good records are important. Keep bills, statements and other documentation showing qualifying expenses and submit them as directed.
Coverage timing matters
Meeting a spend-down can affect when Medicaid coverage becomes active during the applicable period. Do not assume a spend-down notice means full Medicaid coverage is already active.

wisdomArticles.title: What Are Connecticut Medicaid HCBS Programs and Waivers?

blocks.text: “Medicaid waiver” is often used as though it describes one program. Connecticut has multiple home and community-based pathways, and the right one depends on the individual.
HCBS means support in the community
Home and Community-Based Services are designed to help eligible people receive long-term supports in home or community settings rather than relying solely on institutional care.
There is not one universal Medicaid waiver
Connecticut has multiple HCBS pathways serving different populations and needs. Each can have its own functional, financial, programmatic and availability requirements.
Medicaid eligibility and service authorization are not identical
Being financially eligible for Medicaid does not automatically guarantee a particular service, provider, number of hours or waiver placement. Program agencies make those determinations.
Applications are handled through designated processes

Connecticut DSS currently directs new Medicaid applications for home- and community-based waiver services through its LTSS process, with the Greater Hartford LTSS Application Center processing new HCBS Medicaid waiver applications statewide.
Planning at home still requires documentation

wisdomArticles.title: What Is Patient Liability in Connecticut Medicaid LTSS?

blocks.text: A Medicaid approval notice can still show an amount the recipient must contribute toward care. Understanding that contribution can prevent billing confusion.

The calculation depends on the case
DSS applies Medicaid rules to income and allowable deductions. The amount can differ based on circumstances such as marital status and permitted deductions.

Read the DSS notice carefully
The notice should be reviewed for the effective date, amount and any deductions or allocations reflected. A question about the calculation should be raised promptly.

wisdomArticles.title: What Is the Difference Between Medicaid Eligibility and Estate Recovery?

blocks.text: Families often combine two separate Medicaid concepts: qualifying for benefits now and what may happen to an estate later. Understanding the distinction is especially important when a home is involved.
Two different questions

Medicaid eligibility asks whether a person meets the requirements for coverage and services now. Estate recovery concerns circumstances in which the state may later seek repayment from an estate for certain Medicaid costs.
An asset can be treated differently at different stages
A home may receive special treatment during eligibility, yet that does not automatically answer what may happen after the Medicaid recipient dies.
Do not equate “exempt” with “untouchable”
Families sometimes hear that a home is exempt and conclude there can never be a later claim. Eligibility exclusions and estate-recovery rules serve different purposes.
Spouses and other circumstances matter
Federal and state protections and limitations can affect recovery. The facts of the estate, ownership and survivors matter, and legal analysis may be necessary.
Estate planning belongs with an attorney
